en_summary: $GS CEO: The people developing AI models and infrastructure have to take responsibility for what they're building so that it works and doesn't do harm. Companies embedding them must be responsible for deployment and impact. Goldman Sachs has used AI-type models for trading for almost 20 years with human accountability attached to every platform. We wouldn't deploy if we didn't have control and a human accountable for anything that goes wrong.
text:
$GS CEO: "The people that are developing these [AI] models and the infrastructure that allow the technology to exist and ultimately be deployed in the economy have to take responsibility for what they're building, and that it works, and that it doesn't do harm. And then the companies that take those products and embed them in their enterprises and their service have to be responsible for the way they're deployed and the impact that they have.

"And the third is not getting as much attention, but it's equally important. Goldman Sachs has been using AI-type models for trading platforms for almost 20 years, but there's human accountability attached to every one of those platforms.

"I could never imagine someone at Goldman Sachs saying to me, "The trading platform went off and did something awful on its own. We couldn't stop it." We wouldn't deploy it if we didn't feel that we had the control to manage it appropriately, and that there was a human being that was ultimately accountable for anything that goes wrong."

CapEx arms race without compelling returns until early-to-mid 2027 is the main issue. On valuation, AMZN looks cheap at 2027 P/E of 22.1x (EV/EBITDA 9.2x) vs 14% long-term revenue growth and +16% eps growth.
text:

IMO, the CapEx arms race without being able to show compelling returns until early-to-mid 2027 is the main issue holding back investors from buying the $AMZN dip.

On valuation, AMZN looks cheap at a 2027 P/E of 22.1x (EV/EBITDA 9.2x) vs 14% long-term revenue growth and +16% eps growth.

en_summary: $AMZN + $GOOGL reported and their stocks sold off hard. Neither is slowing the AI build. Alphabet maintained $195–205B 2026 capex guide, spending will rise significantly in 2027. Cloud revenue more than doubled. Amazon held ~$220B 2026 capex, Jassy said will spend meaningfully more next year. AWS grew 39% with 40%+ growth guided for 2027 and 2028. Market reacting to Search miss and sluggish ecommerce, and cash burn, not AI slowdown. The gap is the opportunity.
text:
$AMZN + $GOOGL reported and their stocks sold off hard.

Neither is slowing the AI build.

Alphabet maintained its $195–205B 2026 capex guide and said spending will rise "significantly" in 2027. Cloud revenue more than doubled.

Amazon held its ~$220B 2026 capex guide and Jassy said they will spend “meaningfully more” next year. AWS grew 39%  (fastest in nearly five years) with 40%+ growth guided for 2027 and 2028.

The market is reacting to a Search miss at Google and sluggish ecommerce growth at Amazon; and to cash burn, not to a slowdown in AI infrastructure demand.

The people building the capacity are still accelerating. The market is focused on the near-term bill. That gap is the opportunity.

en_summary: @StockSavvyShay thinks the market is underestimating $NOW, because even if $GOOGL Gemini or ChatGPT becomes the interface employees use, that does not replace the systems doing the actual work. He finds Action Fabric interesting because outside AI agents can tap its enterprise data and workflows, and the company could earn more revenue as those agents complete more tasks. An image is attached.
text:
I think the market is underestimating $NOW because even if $GOOGL Gemini or ChatGPT becomes interface employees use it doesn't mean they replace the systems doing the actual work.

That's where Action Fabric gets really interesting because outside AI agents can tap into its enterprise data and workflows while the company could earn more revenue as those agents complete more tasks.
